state: A landlord offers a 10% discount for 6 months' rent upfront.

options.text: Pay 6 months upfront.
Pay monthly per the contract.
Ask for the discount without prepayment.

reference.rationale_short: Prepayment locks money without protection; the discount is not worth the risk.
reference.rationale_full: Six rents upfront means the landlord holds your money while you hold no leverage if anything breaks or he sells the flat. A 10% discount is smaller than the risk of losing the whole prepayment. Monthly payment per contract keeps money and rights; a discount can be negotiated through a longer lease instead.

state: A friend asks you to co-sign a 20,000 loan.

options.text: Sign because they are a friend.
Decline co-signing and help differently.
Sign on condition they pay you first.

reference.rationale_short: A co-signer owes as if they borrowed; friendship does not change that.
reference.rationale_full: Co-signing is not a recommendation but a guarantee: if the friend stops paying, the bank collects the full amount plus interest from you, no questions asked. A 'pay me first' condition is unenforceable when money runs out. Real help is a smaller loan you can forgive or budgeting help — not a signature binding you for years.

state: An employer offers a 20% raise for switching to night shifts.

options.text: Accept at once for the money.
Ask for a trial month of nights with a right to return.
Refuse without thinking.

reference.rationale_short: Nights do not suit everyone; a trial with an exit before a permanent call.
reference.rationale_full: Twenty percent more sounds good until night shifts are tried: sleep, family and health cost more. Refusing without a trial may waste a good chance, and accepting without an exit locks in. A trial month with a written right to return to days gives facts instead of guessing.

state: A bank offers a credit card with a 'free' first year and a 5000 limit.

options.text: Take it since the first year is free.
Read the post-year rates and fees, then decide.
Refuse all cards forever.

reference.rationale_short: The free year is bait; the real price is the rate from year two.
reference.rationale_full: Banks do not gift cards: profit is interest on debt plus annual fees from year two on. Skipping the terms means paying them with interest. Refusal on principle is legitimate but may waste a useful reserve; reading the fine print first is the only rational path.

state: A neighbour builds a fence 30 cm over the boundary while you are at work.

options.text: Tear the fence down the same evening.
Photograph it, call a surveyor, demand restoration.
Tolerate it to keep relations.

reference.rationale_short: Boundaries are proven on paper, not with a hammer; tolerance loses land over time.
reference.rationale_full: Thirty centimetres today becomes a metre tomorrow, and years of tolerance lead to adverse possession. Demolition is property damage putting you in the wrong. A survey report plus a written demand, then the inspectorate — paper returns land, hammers bring charges.

state: A doctor recommends a pricey private scan though a free public alternative exists.

options.text: Pay private since the doctor knows best.
Ask why the public option falls short; seek a second opinion.
Refuse every scan.

reference.rationale_short: A private referral may be commission; one question plus a second opinion clarifies.
reference.rationale_full: A doctor sending you private may have a deal with the clinic — or honestly believe it is better. One question reveals the difference: what exactly does the public option not cover? If unconvinced, a second opinion costs less than the scan. Refusing everything risks health over suspicion.

state: A market seller issues no receipt for a 500 purchase.

options.text: Buy receipt-free since it is cheaper.
Condition the purchase on a fiscal receipt.
Report them without buying.

reference.rationale_short: No receipt means no warranty claim; a fiscal receipt protects the buyer.
reference.rationale_full: Five hundred without paper means: defects cannot be claimed, origin unproven, and you join tax evasion. Reporting without buying is legitimate but solves nothing for your purchase. A fiscal receipt costs the seller tax and gives you a guarantee — condition the purchase on it.

state: A firm delays wages a second month; the boss promises 'everything at once soon'.

options.text: Trust and wait.
Demand a written pay date and learn your rights.
Quit the same day.

reference.rationale_short: A dateless promise is stalling; a paper trail protects, quitting blind harms.
reference.rationale_full: A second delayed month with a vague promise is a pattern, not an exception — the firm may be sinking. Trust without a trace leaves no evidence for disputes. Quitting the same day loses severance and benefits. A written deadline plus knowing your rights (inspectorate, claims) keeps every option open.

state: A car overheats on the motorway in summer; the rest area is 5 km away.

options.text: Drive on slowly to the rest area.
Stop at once on the shoulder and kill the engine.
Speed up to arrive before failure.

reference.rationale_short: An overheated engine stops at once; every kilometre risks a rebuild or fire.
reference.rationale_full: The needle in the red means cooling has failed — driving on melts the head gasket (a rebuild) or sets the engine alight. Five kilometres is too far for an overheated engine. Shoulder, engine off, bonnet up, wait — a tow costs less than an engine.

state: A tenant smells gas leaking in the building; the odour fills the hallway.

options.text: Flip lights on to see where it leaks.
Touch no switches, open doors, exit and call emergency.
Wait for someone else to react.

reference.rationale_short: A switch spark ignites gas; exiting and calling saves the building.
reference.rationale_full: Gas in the hallway waits only for a spark — and a light switch makes one. Flipping switches 'to inspect' is the most dangerous move. The protocol is fixed: nothing electric, ventilate by opening, exit, call the gas emergency line and the manager from outside. Waiting wastes deciding minutes.

state: A diner finds a fly in the soup halfway through the bowl.

options.text: Eat the rest to avoid a scene.
Send it back, ask for a replacement or removal from the bill.
Leave without paying the whole bill.

reference.rationale_short: Guests pay for correct food; a replacement or discount is standard.
reference.rationale_full: A fly in the soup is the kitchen's fault, not the guest's shame — swallowing it out of politeness pays for their mistake. Walking out on the whole bill (drinks, bread) is dishonest the other way. A calm complaint gets a replacement or the item removed; restaurants expect and budget for it.

state: A worker finds a wallet with 1000 on a site with no witnesses.

options.text: Keep it, finders keepers.
Hand it to the foreman with a record, or the police.
Take half, report the rest.

reference.rationale_short: Finding confers no ownership; a record also shields against colleagues' suspicion.
reference.rationale_full: The rule is clear: a finder who keeps commits embezzlement, and on a site word gets around who was there. Half-and-half is the same theft with maths. Handing it over with a record (foreman, police) is not only lawful but shields against suspicion — and honest finders often get rewarded.

state: A student is offered a finished thesis for 300, 'guaranteed to pass'.

options.text: Buy it, cheaper than repeating the year.
Decline and write it with a mentor.
Report the seller to the faculty.

reference.rationale_short: A bought thesis fails at defence and checks; mentorship is the legal path.
reference.rationale_full: A bought thesis is spotted at defence in five minutes — the student cannot explain 'their own' text, and plagiarism checks catch recycling. The price of discovery is expulsion and a study ban. Reporting the seller is civic duty but solves nothing for the student; writing with a mentor is the only path giving both degree and knowledge.

state: A driver clips a parked car unseen; damage is a small scratch.

options.text: Leave since nobody saw.
Leave your number under the wiper and report to insurance.
Wait hours for the owner.

reference.rationale_short: Leaving the scene is an offence; a number under the wiper solves everything in a minute.
reference.rationale_full: Cameras see everything today — leaving 'because nobody saw' becomes hit-and-run with a fine bigger than the damage. Waiting hours is honest but impractical. A phone number under the wiper plus a photo and an insurance report: the owner calls, the damage is paid from cover, everyone calm.

state: A patient waits 4 hours for an urgent exam; the desk says 'be patient'.

options.text: Go home and come tomorrow.
Ask the triage nurse for a written urgency assessment.
Storm into the office by force.

reference.rationale_short: Urgency is triaged, not desk-judged; a paper trail forces the system.
reference.rationale_full: Four hours for 'urgent' means triage failed or the system is broken — either way the desk answer is not authoritative. Going home risks deterioration, storming in is an offence. The triage nurse assesses urgency professionally, and a written request creates accountability.

state: A seller refuses a warranty claim on 5-day-old tech with no reason.

options.text: Accept the refusal.
Demand the refusal in writing, then the market inspectorate.
Make a scene in the shop.

reference.rationale_short: Five days is within every warranty; a paper trail then the inspectorate.
reference.rationale_full: Five-day-old tech is fully under warranty — an unexplained verbal refusal is a bluff counting on the buyer giving up. Accepting loses money, a scene is an offence. A written refusal (or a record of them refusing one) plus a market inspectorate report settles it for the buyer.

state: A neighbour's dog barks all night for a week; talking did not help.

options.text: Poison the dog.
Report to municipal police with a noise log.
Endure it and buy earplugs.

reference.rationale_short: Night noise is the owner's offence; poisoning is a crime.
reference.rationale_full: A week of sleepless nights grants no right to revenge on the animal — poisoning is a criminal offence punished harder than any noise. Earplugs surrender without solving the cause. A noise log (dates, recordings) plus a municipal police report forces the owner to train or pay fines.

state: A firm offers a job with no written contract, 'all agreed verbally'.

options.text: Start since pay is needed.
Condition the start on a written contract.
Work a month, then ask for a contract.

reference.rationale_short: No contract means no pay, seniority or protection; a month unpapered is a gift.
reference.rationale_full: A verbal deal in court is worth as much as witnesses who vanish when needed. A month of work 'then we will see' gives the employer free labour and an excuse to never have hired you. A written contract before day one: pay, hours, notice. Without it — no job.

state: An ATM swallows a card on Friday night; the bank opens Monday.

options.text: Try fishing the card out yourself.
Block the card in the app, collect a new one Monday.
Wait the weekend with no money.

reference.rationale_short: A swallowed card is not necessarily safe; an in-app block takes a minute.
reference.rationale_full: ATMs retain cards for reasons — expiry, suspicion, error — and Friday night means 60 unsupervised hours. Fishing it out yourself damages the machine (your liability). Block in the mobile app at once, then a new card Monday; the weekend survives on cash or a second card.

state: A call from an unknown number: 'you won a prize, just confirm your details'.

options.text: Give details since it is a prize.
Hang up and block the number.
Ask for written prize confirmation.

reference.rationale_short: Prizes are never handed out via phone interrogation; hanging up is the only safe reply.
reference.rationale_full: No legitimate prize asks for details by phone from an unknown number — that is the definition of phishing. Giving any single detail opens identity theft. Written confirmation sounds careful, but the call itself is the trap (voice recorded for scams). Hang up and block, no exceptions.

state: Water leaks from the ceiling at the neighbour below; they knock in panic.

options.text: Say it is not your problem.
Shut your valves, check the bathroom, call a plumber.
Wait till morning.

reference.rationale_short: Water does not wait for morning; your valve and a plumber limit damage you pay for.
reference.rationale_full: A downstairs leak comes from your flat 9 times in 10 — and the causer pays the damage. Denial does not stop water, waiting till morning multiplies damage (and the bill). Shutting your valves, a quick bathroom check and the on-call plumber: every minute less water is thousands less damage.

state: A child swallows a coin; breathes normally but complains of throat pain.

options.text: Induce vomiting to bring it up.
To emergency for imaging; no food.
Wait for it to pass naturally.

reference.rationale_short: A coin (a battery above all) eats the oesophagus wall within hours; image at once.
reference.rationale_full: A swallowed metal object is not harmless: if it is a button battery, current and chemistry pierce the oesophagus in hours. Vomiting returns the object through the gullet a second time (double damage). Waiting gambles with time. Emergency, imaging, no food — the doctor decides removal or monitoring.

state: A basement floods at night; water pushes through the small windows.

options.text: Go down to save belongings.
Cut basement power, call firefighters and the manager.
Wait till morning.

reference.rationale_short: Water plus basement power kills; belongings are not saved with lives.
reference.rationale_full: Basement water plus wiring is a deadly mix — entering for boxes risks electrocution in the dark. Waiting till morning lets water reach meters and lifts. Cutting basement power (staircase switch), calling firefighters for pumps and the manager — in that order.

state: Power is out, the fridge is full, summer, 35 degrees; the fault lasts till evening.

options.text: Open the fridge to check the state.
Keep the fridge shut; eat perishables first once power returns.
Throw everything out at once.

reference.rationale_short: A shut fridge holds cold for hours; every opening loses it.
reference.rationale_full: A full unopened fridge holds safe temperature 4-6 hours even powerless — every 'check' lets cold out and shortens that span. Throwing everything out at once wastes money before anything spoils. Keep shut, and once power returns eat/cook perishables first (meat, milk), sniff-check the rest.

state: A dodgy 'bank' message asks for the PIN to 'verify the account'.

options.text: Send the PIN since it is urgent.
Delete it and report to the bank on the official number.
Call the number from the message to verify.

reference.rationale_short: Banks never ask for PINs by message; delete and report via the official channel.
reference.rationale_full: The golden rule of banking: the PIN is given to nobody, never, not even the bank — and least of all by message. Calling the message's number connects straight to the scammers. Real verification runs in reverse: you call the bank on the card's number and ask whether anything was requested.

state: A tyre bursts on the motorway at 120 km/h; the car pulls.

options.text: Brake hard to a stop.
Lift off, hold straight firmly, slow onto the shoulder.
Veer sharply into the right lane.

reference.rationale_short: Hard braking or swerving with a burst tyre rolls the car; straight and gradual.
reference.rationale_full: A high-speed blowout is the most dangerous moment: hard braking shifts weight and yaws the car, a sharp swerve rolls it. Hands firm on the wheel, straight line, foot off the gas, gentle braking only as speed drops — the shoulder arrives itself.

state: A stray dog follows a child home from school every day this week.

options.text: Feed it to befriend it.
Report to animal control and walk the child.
Chase it off with stones.

reference.rationale_short: A stray near a child is a bite risk; control catches, feeding binds the dog to the child.
reference.rationale_full: A dog that 'just follows' today may bite tomorrow when another child pulls its tail — and strays carry rabies risk. Feeding binds it permanently to the child's route. Stoning teaches fear of children (then fear-biting). Report to control plus walking the child until resolved.

state: A child brings home a bad grade and hides the test from the parents.

options.text: Punish harshly for lying and the grade.
Talk: praise honesty when admitted first, then a study plan.
Ignore it since it is one grade.

reference.rationale_short: Harsh punishment teaches hiding, not learning; talk plus a plan fixes the cause.
reference.rationale_full: A child hiding a test already fears the reaction — harsh punishment confirms the fear and next time they will lie better. Ignoring signals grades do not matter. The right order: when admitted, first acknowledge the courage of honesty, then a joint plan (what was unknown, when to practise) — the grade recovers, trust stays.

state: A school asks consent for a 800 trip abroad.

options.text: Sign so the child is not excluded.
Check the programme, insurance and cancellation terms first.
Refuse since it is costly.

reference.rationale_short: A peer-pressure signature costs; programme and insurance before signing.
reference.rationale_full: Eight hundred on a signature 'so the child fits in' is the costliest reason. The real question has three parts: what the children get (programme), who answers if something happens (insurance, escorts) and what quitting costs (cancellation terms). Only with all three answers — sign or refuse, both legitimate.

state: A used-fridge seller claims 'like new' but gives no warranty or receipt.

options.text: Buy since it looks new.
Demand a trial run and a written deal, or walk away.
Pay a deposit by phone.

reference.rationale_short: 'Like new' without paper is talk; a trial run reveals compressor and noise.
reference.rationale_full: Fridges are not bought by eye: compressor, thermostat and seals are proven by running, not looks. 'Like new' with no warranty means the seller does not stand behind the words. An hour's trial run (does it cool, is it loud) plus a written return deal — or walk away. A phone deposit is a gift to a stranger.
